summary:
Piauí stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people and shows no documented state-level deviation, so a trans visitor's status, documents and family recognition are handled under the same national-judicial rules that apply elsewhere in the country. Piauí's own courts have issued gender recognition; a 2021 record documents recognition granted through the state's judiciary.

Legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or medical diagnosis, under the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018, and proceeds by self-determination. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, with joint adoption available since 2010 and full adoption rights since 2015.

Discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity are a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, following the Supreme Federal Court's decision of 13 June 2019, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Courts have applied that framework to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.

Documents remain binary. Brazil has no third-gender option nationwide, so a neutral or X marker on a foreign passport has no counterpart in Brazilian civil records. Civil registries have accepted non-binary or unspecified entries since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent, with practice varying between states.

Detention is governed by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; placement is fixed by a reasoned decision taken after the person has been consulted about their preference, and LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation. Practice diverges from that text: a census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates across eleven units in Rio de Janeiro state and found them housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units.

An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family matters are treated on the same footing as anyone else's at entry.
tangentialFactors:
OutRight International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and that the legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress.

Targeted violence has been documented in settings a visitor would use. A May 2024 investigation recorded 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Protection machinery has widened in ways that matter to residents and visitors alike. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

State-level rules on custodial treatment differ in practice and in text. Rio de Janeiro state law of 2015 grants trans women parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, alongside national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. The same system nonetheless held travestis and trans women in masculine-operated units, which the 2021 census describes as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights.
localsOnly:
Trans voters may register to vote under their lived name and identity even before their identity documents are updated, so electoral participation does not depend on completed legal gender change.

Political visibility is documented at national level: over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, and the first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Civil-registry practice for residents has moved beyond the binary option. Non-binary or unspecified entries have been possible since 2020, and the Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent, though the availability of such entries continues to vary state by state.

Family law operates on the same terms as for anyone else: same-sex marriage since the 2013 National Council of Justice resolution, joint adoption since 2010, full adoption rights since 2015. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination with no surgery, hormones or diagnosis required.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Piauí-specific record of anti-LGBT violence, hate-crime prosecutions or police handling is sourced for this entry; the documented incidents and violence rates in the surrounding text come from other states and from national reporting.

Whether the placement rules of National Council of Justice Resolution 348 and Resolution 366 have been applied inside Piauí's custodial facilities is unresolved here, and no study of Piauí detention practice appears in the inventory.

Whether the Superior Court of Justice neutral-gender precedent of 6 May 2025 has been used by civil registries in Piauí is not sourced, as is the availability of non-binary entries in the state's own registries.

The repeal pressure described by OutRight International is asserted in general terms; no specific bill or provision targeting trans people is named in the sources.

Claims of a world-highest toll of killings of trans people and of protections thinning outside major cities appear in the national context only, and are not tied to Piauí by any source in this inventory.
